The '''no–no paradox''' is a distinctive [[paradox]] belonging to the family of the [[semantics|semantic]] paradoxes (like the [[Liar paradox]]). It derives its name from the fact that it consists of two sentences each simply denying what the other says.

{{TOC limit|3}}

==History==

A variation on the paradox occurs already in [[Thomas Bradwardine]]’s ''Insolubilia''.<ref>Bradwardine, T. (1970), ''Insolubilia'', pp. 304–305, in Roure, M.-L. (1970). ‘La problématique des propositions insolubles au XIII<sup>e</sup> siècle et au début du XIV<sup>e</sup>, suivie de l’édition des traités de W. Shyreswood, W. Burleigh et Th. Bradwardine’, ''Archives d’Histoire Doctrinale et Littéraire du Moyen Âge'' '''37''', pp. 205–326.</ref> The paradox itself appears as the eighth sophism of chapter 8 of [[John Buridan]]’s ''Sophismata''.<ref>Buridan, J. (2001), ''Summulae de Dialectica'', tr. G. Klima, New Haven: Yale University Press, p. 971.</ref> Although the paradox went largely unnoticed even during 20th-century revival of semantic paradoxes, it has recently been rediscovered (and dubbed with its current name) by the American philosopher [[Roy Sorensen]],<ref>Sorensen, R. (2001), ''Vagueness and Contradiction'', Oxford: Oxford University Press.</ref> and is now appreciated for the distinctive difficulties it presents.<ref>Greenough, P. (2011), 'Truthmaker gaps and the no-no paradox', ''Philosophy and Phenomenological Research'' '''82''', pp. 547–563.</ref>

==Formulation==

The notion of [[truth]] seems to be governed by the naive schema:

:(T): The sentence ' ''P'' ' is true if and only if ''P''

(where we use single quotes to refer to the linguistic expression inside the quotes). Consider however the two sentences:

:(N<sub>1</sub>): (N<sub>2</sub>) is not true

:(N<sub>2</sub>): (N<sub>1</sub>) is not true

Reasoning in [[classical logic]], there are four possibilities concerning (N<sub>1</sub>) and (N<sub>2</sub>):

# Both (N<sub>1</sub>) and (N<sub>2</sub>) are true
# Both (N<sub>1</sub>) and (N<sub>2</sub>) are not true
# (N<sub>1</sub>) is true and (N<sub>2</sub>) is not true
# (N<sub>1</sub>) is not true and (N<sub>2</sub>) is true

Yet, possibilities 1. and 2. are ruled out by the instances of (T) for (N<sub>1</sub>) and (N<sub>2</sub>). To wit, possibility 1. is ruled out because, if (N<sub>1</sub>) is true, then, by (T), (N<sub>2</sub>) is not true; possibility 2. is ruled out because, if (N<sub>1</sub>) is not true, then, by (T), (N<sub>2</sub>) is true. It would then seem that either of possibilities 3. and 4. should obtain. Yet, both of those possibilities would also seem repugnant, as, on each of them, two perfectly symmetrical sentences would mysteriously diverge in [[truth value]].

==Discussion==

Generally speaking, the paradox instantiates the problem of determining the status of ungrounded sentences that are not [[consistency|inconsistent]].<ref>Herzberger, H. (1970), 'Paradoxes of grounding in semantics', ''The Journal of Philosophy'' '''67''', pp. 145–167</ref> More in particular, the paradox presents the challenge of expanding one’s favourite theory of truth with further principles which either express the symmetry intuition against possibilities 3. and 4.<ref>Priest, G. (2005), 'Words without knowledge', ''Philosophy and Phenomenological Research'' '''71''', pp. 686–694.</ref> or make them acceptable in spite of their intuitive repugnancy.<ref>Sorensen, R. (2001), ''Vagueness and Contradiction'', Oxford: Oxford University Press, pp. 165–184.</ref> Because (N<sub>1</sub>) and (N<sub>2</sub>) do not lead to inconsistency, a certain strand in the discussion of the paradox has been willing to assume both the relevant instances of (T) and classical logic, thereby deriving the conclusion that either possibility 3. or possibility 4. holds.<ref>Armour-Garb, B. and J. Woodbridge (2006), 'Dialetheism, semantic pathology, and the open pair', ''Australasian Journal of Philosophy'' '''84''', pp. 395–416.</ref> Such conclusion has in turn been taken to have momentous consequences for certain influential philosophical theses. Consider, for example, the thesis of [[truthmaker]] maximalism:

:(TM): If a sentence is true, there is something that makes it true<ref>Armstrong, D. (2004), ''Truth and Truth-Makers'', Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.</ref>

If, as per possibilities 3. and 4., one of (N<sub>1</sub>) or (N<sub>2</sub>) is true and the other one is not true, then, given the symmetry between the two sentences, it might seem that there is nothing that makes true whichever of the two is in fact true. If so, (TM) would fail.<ref>Sorensen, R. (2001), ''Vagueness and Contradiction'', Oxford: Oxford University Press, p. 176.</ref> These and similar conclusions have however been contested by other philosophers on the grounds that, as evidenced by [[Curry's paradox]], joint reliance on (T) and classical logic might be problematic even when it does not lead to inconsistency.<ref>López de Sa, D. and E. Zardini (2007), 'Truthmakers, knowledge and paradox', ''Analysis'' '''67''', pp. 242–250.</ref>
